title: Nearest-Neighbor Radii under Dependent Sampling
claim: Estimated moment-scaling slopes track the theoretical p/d line under weak dependence but deviate systematically as dependence strengthens.
layout: 3x3 grid of line plots, rows by dimension, columns by model, shared legend
description: A 3x3 grid of line plots. Columns are three dependent model classes: Linear State Space, Hidden Markov Model, and FFT Stationary GP (RBF-like). Rows are intrinsic dimension d=1, 3 and 5. Each panel plots estimated slope on the y-axis against moment order p on the x-axis. A shared legend at the bottom shows a dotted gray theory line p/d, a black iid line with diamonds, and weak (green stars), medium (orange squares) and strong (blue circles) dependence. In most panels the iid and weak curves lie on the theory line. Medium and strong curves deviate, either above it (HMM, and strong in the d=1 linear model) or below it (GP and higher-d linear). The deviation is largest at high p. The eye goes first to the diverging orange and blue curves in the top row.
caption: Slope summary for Experiment 1: rows correspond to d = 1, 3, 5, columns correspond to the three dependent model classes, and the shared legend compares the theoretical line p/d, the i.i.d. benchmark, and weak/medium/strong dependence.
abstract: Nearest-neighbor methods are fundamental to classical and modern machine learning, yet their geometric properties are typically analyzed under independent sampling. In this paper, we study the nearest-neighbor radii under dependent sampling. We consider strong mixing dependent observations and ask whether dependence changes the scale of nearest-neighbor neighborhoods. We establish distribution-free almost sure convergence under polynomial mixing and sharp non-asymptotic moment bounds under geometric mixing. The moment bounds depend on the local intrinsic dimension rather than the ambient dimension, making the results applicable to high-dimensional data supported on lower-dimensional manifolds. Synthetic experiments and real-world time-series benchmarks illustrate the theory, showing that nearest-neighbor geometry remains informative under dependent sampling.
